Name: 2G
Definition: In the context of telecommunications, 2nd Generation (2G) refers to the second generation of mobile network technology standards. 2G networks were introduced in the early 1990s as an evolution from the first generation (1G) analog cellular networks. The transition to 2G brought significant improvements in terms of digital voice quality, data services, and network capacity. Key features of 2G networks include: Digital Voice : 2G networks introduced digital voice encoding, which improved call quality and reduced interference compared to analog systems. Data Services : 2G networks enabled basic data services such as SMS (Short Message Service) and MMS (Multimedia Messaging Service). Security : Enhanced security features such as encryption were introduced in 2G networks to protect user communications. Global System for Mobile Communications (GSM) : The most widely adopted 2G technology, GSM standardized network protocols and allowed for interoperability between different operators and regions. Some of the popular 2G technologies include: GSM (Global System for Mobile Communications) : Widely deployed 2G technology globally. CDMA (Code Division Multiple Access) : Another 2G technology used in some regions, especially in North America. While 2G networks paved the way for digital mobile communications and basic data services, they were eventually succeeded by newer generations of mobile networks such as 3G, 4G, and now 5G. These subsequent generations brought further advancements in data speeds, network capacity, and support for advanced services like mobile internet, video streaming, and IoT (Internet of Things) connectivity.

Name: 3G
Definition: In the realm of telecommunications, the 3rd Generation (3G) represents the third iteration of mobile network technology standards. 3G networks were introduced in the early 2000s as an advancement over 2G networks, offering higher data speeds, improved voice quality, and enhanced multimedia capabilities. Key features and advancements of 3G networks include: Higher Data Speeds : 3G networks provided significantly faster data speeds compared to 2G, enabling services like mobile internet browsing, video streaming, and video calling. Enhanced Multimedia Support : 3G networks supported multimedia services such as video calls, mobile TV, and music streaming. Wider Coverage and Capacity : 3G networks expanded network coverage and capacity, allowing for more users to connect simultaneously and access data-intensive services. Packet-Switched Data : 3G networks introduced packet-switched data transmission, which improved efficiency in handling data traffic. Some of the prominent 3G technologies include: UMTS (Universal Mobile Telecommunications System) : A widely deployed 3G technology based on the WCDMA (Wideband Code Division Multiple Access) standard. CDMA2000 : Another 3G technology used in some regions, particularly in North America and parts of Asia. 3G networks played a crucial role in the evolution of mobile communications by enabling a wide range of data services and paving the way for the mobile internet era. However, with the rapid growth of data consumption and the demand for higher data speeds, 3G networks have been gradually phased out in favor of newer generations of mobile networks such as 4G LTE and 5G, which offer even faster speeds, lower latency, and enhanced capabilities to support emerging technologies like IoT and augmented reality.

Name: 3GPP
Definition: 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) refers to a global telecommunications collaboration that aims to develop standards and specifications for mobile communications systems. It brings together various organizations from different regions to establish guidelines for the design, deployment, and operation of wireless networks and technologies. Its focus is on enabling seamless connectivity, interoperability, and efficient use of resources across different generations of mobile networks.

Name: 4G
Definition: In the telecommunications industry, the 4th Generation (4G) represents the fourth iteration of mobile network technology standards. 4G networks were introduced in the late 2000s and early 2010s as a significant advancement over 3G networks, offering faster data speeds, lower latency, and improved network efficiency. Key features and advancements of 4G networks include: High-Speed Data : 4G networks deliver significantly faster data speeds than 3G, enabling seamless streaming of high-definition video, online gaming, and faster downloads. Low Latency : 4G networks have lower latency, reducing the delay in data transmission and improving real-time communication applications like video calls and online gaming. IP-Based Network : 4G networks are based on IP (Internet Protocol), allowing for seamless integration with the internet and supporting a wide range of IP-based services and applications. Efficient Spectrum Utilization : 4G technologies use spectrum more efficiently, enabling higher data capacity and better network performance. Some of the prominent 4G technologies include: LTE (Long-Term Evolution) : The most widely deployed 4G technology, offering high data speeds and low latency. WiMAX (Worldwide Interoperability for Microwave Access) : Another 4G technology that provides wireless broadband access. 4G networks have revolutionized mobile communications by enabling a wide range of data-intensive services and applications, including mobile broadband, video streaming, cloud services, and IoT connectivity. The widespread adoption of 4G has laid the foundation for the digital transformation of industries and the proliferation of connected devices. As the demand for faster speeds and more advanced services continues to grow, the telecommunications industry has been transitioning to the next generation of mobile networks, 5G, which promises even higher data speeds, ultra-low latency, and support for emerging technologies like autonomous vehicles, smart cities, and industrial automation.

Name: 5G

Name: 5G-GUTI
Definition: The 5G Globally Unique Temporary Identifier (GUTI) is a key element in 5G mobile networks that serves as a temporary identifier for a user equipment (UE) when it connects to the network. The GUTI is used to uniquely identify and authenticate the UE within the 5G network, allowing for secure and efficient communication between the UE and the network. Here are some key points about the 5G GUTI: Temporary Identifier : The GUTI is temporary and is assigned to the UE when it attaches to the 5G network. It is used during the initial registration process and while the UE is connected to the network. Global Uniqueness : The GUTI is globally unique, meaning that no two UEs in the 5G network will have the same GUTI. This uniqueness ensures that each UE can be identified and managed individually. Privacy Protection : The GUTI plays a role in protecting the privacy of the UE by concealing its permanent identity (such as the International Mobile Subscriber Identity or IMSI) from external entities in the network. Security : The GUTI is used in the authentication and security procedures between the UE and the network to ensure that only authorized UEs can access the network and that communication is secure. Mobility Management : The GUTI is essential for mobility management in 5G networks, allowing the network to track the UE's location, manage handovers between cells, and maintain seamless connectivity as the UE moves within the network. Overall, the 5G GUTI plays a critical role in the operation of 5G networks by providing a temporary and globally unique identifier for UEs, ensuring privacy protection, security, and efficient mobility management. It is an essential component that enables secure and reliable communication between UEs and the 5G network infrastructure

Name: 5GACIA
Definition: 5G for Connected Industries and Automation, often referred to as Industrial 5G, is a key application of 5G technology that aims to transform industries by enabling advanced connectivity, automation, and digitalization. Industrial 5G leverages the capabilities of 5G networks to support a wide range of use cases and applications in sectors such as manufacturing, transportation, energy, healthcare, and agriculture. Key benefits and features of 5G for Connected Industries and Automation include: Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communication (URLLC) : 5G networks provide ultra-low latency and high reliability, making them suitable for mission-critical applications in industrial automation, robotics, and remote control systems. Massive Machine-Type Communication (mMTC) : 5G supports the connectivity of a massive number of IoT devices and sensors, enabling real-time data collection, monitoring, and control in industrial environments. Network Slicing : Industrial 5G allows for the creation of dedicated network slices tailored to specific industrial use cases, ensuring optimized performance, security, and resource allocation. Edge Computing : By combining 5G with edge computing capabilities, industrial applications can benefit from low-latency data processing and real-time decision-making at the network edge. Smart Manufacturing : 5G enables smart factories with connected machines, predictive maintenance, remote monitoring, and automation of production processes for increased efficiency and productivity. Autonomous Vehicles and Drones : Industrial 5G supports autonomous vehicles, drones, and mobile robots in industrial settings, enabling autonomous navigation, real-time communication, and coordination. Remote Maintenance and Diagnostics : 5G facilitates remote maintenance, troubleshooting, and diagnostics of industrial equipment and machinery, reducing downtime and improving operational efficiency. Augmented Reality (AR) and Virtual Reality (VR) : Industrial 5G enables immersive AR/VR applications for training, remote assistance, and visualization of complex data in industrial environments. Industrial 5G has the potential to revolutionize industries by enabling digital transformation, automation, and the adoption of Industry 4.0 principles. It offers opportunities for increased efficiency, flexibility, and innovation in industrial processes, leading to improved productivity, cost savings, and new business models. As industries continue to adopt and leverage the capabilities of 5G networks, the integration of connectivity, automation, and data analytics will drive the next wave of industrial revolution, transforming traditional industries into smart, connected, and agile ecosystems.

Name: 5GC
Definition: The 5G Core (5GC) is the central part of a 5G network architecture that is responsible for managing and orchestrating communication services for 5G devices and users. It serves as the backbone of the 5G network, providing the necessary functions to enable advanced features and capabilities offered by 5G technology. Key components and functions of the 5G Core include: Network Function Services : The 5G Core consists of various network functions that provide essential services such as user authentication, session management, mobility management, and policy control. Service-Based Architecture : 5GC is designed with a service-based architecture that allows network functions to communicate with each other using standardized interfaces, promoting flexibility and scalability. Network Slicing : The 5G Core supports network slicing, which enables the creation of virtual networks tailored to specific use cases or services, ensuring optimal performance and resource allocation. User Plane Function (UPF) : The UPF is responsible for handling user data traffic, routing packets efficiently, and ensuring low latency for data-intensive applications. Session Management : The 5G Core manages user sessions, including the establishment, maintenance, and termination of connections, to enable seamless mobility and service continuity. Policy Control : It enforces policies related to quality of service, network access, and traffic management to optimize network resources and ensure a consistent user experience. Authentication and Security : The 5G Core includes functions for user authentication, encryption, and security to protect user data and privacy in the network. The 5G Core plays a crucial role in enabling advanced 5G services and use cases, such as ultra-reliable low-latency communication (URLLC), massive machine-type communication (mMTC), and enhanced mobile broadband (eMBB). It provides the foundation for innovative applications in sectors like healthcare, transportation, smart cities, and industrial automation that require high-speed connectivity, low latency, and reliable communication. Overall, the 5G Core architecture is designed to support the diverse requirements of 5G networks and applications, offering enhanced performance, flexibility, and efficiency to meet the evolving needs of the digital era.

Definition: Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting in the context of Telecommunications refer to three distinct processes used to manage and secure access to telecommunications networks and systems. It ensures that only authorized individuals or devices are granted access, protecting against unauthorized access and potential security threats.Authorization is the process of granting or denying specific privileges or permissions to authenticated users or devices based on predefined access policies. It ensures that users or devices have the necessary permissions to perform particular actions or access specific resources within the network.Accounting, also known as auditing or logging, involves tracking and recording the activities of authenticated users or devices within the network. It includes collecting information such as the date and time of login, the duration of the connection, and the resources accessed. Accounting helps in monitoring network usage, detecting security breaches or anomalies, and facilitating billing or resource management.These three processes work together to ensure the proper management, security, and control of telecommunications networks and systems.

Name: C-RAN
Definition: A Centralized Radio Access Network (C-RAN) is a network architecture that centralizes the baseband processing of multiple remote radio heads (RRHs) in a centralized location. In a traditional RAN architecture, the baseband processing is typically located at the base of each cell tower or site. However, in a C-RAN architecture, the baseband processing functions are moved to a centralized data center or hub. Key components of a C-RAN architecture include: Remote Radio Heads (RRHs) : These are the radio units located at the cell sites that connect to antennas and transmit/receive radio signals. Baseband Unit (BBU) : The centralized unit that processes the baseband signals from multiple RRHs. It performs functions such as modulation/demodulation, encoding/decoding, and signal processing. Fronthaul Network : The high-capacity network that connects the RRHs at the cell sites to the centralized BBU. Benefits of C-RAN include: Centralized Processing : Allows for more efficient resource allocation and coordination across multiple cells. Cost Savings : By centralizing baseband processing, operators can reduce the number of equipment at cell sites and lower operational costs. Flexibility and Scalability : Easier to scale the network and introduce new technologies by upgrading centralized processing units. Energy Efficiency : Centralized processing can lead to energy savings compared to distributed RAN architectures. C-RAN is seen as a key enabler for future mobile networks, especially in the context of 5G deployments, where centralized processing and coordination are essential for delivering high data rates, low latency, and supporting a massive number of connected devices.

The Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC), the regulatory body overseeing broadcasting in Canada, classifies television channels into different categories based on their programming content, format, and distribution requirements. Category A channels are considered to be more established and have specific regulatory obligations and benefits, including guaranteed distribution and protection from direct competition. Category A channels are subject to certain requirements, such as Canadian content quotas, financial contributions to Canadian programming, and restrictions on the types of programming they can air. These channels play a significant role in the Canadian broadcasting landscape, offering specialized content to viewers and contributing to the diversity of programming available on television. Overall, the Category A classification system helps to regulate and promote the development of specialty channels in Canada, ensuring that viewers have access to a variety of programming options while supporting the production and distribution of Canadian content in the media and entertainment industry.

Category B channels are considered to be more niche or specialized in their programming focus and may not have the same level of distribution as Category A channels. Category B channels have more flexibility in terms of their programming content and format compared to Category A channels. They are still subject to regulatory requirements, such as Canadian content quotas, financial contributions to Canadian programming, and other obligations to support the production and promotion of Canadian content. While Category B channels may not have guaranteed carriage on basic cable or satellite packages, they play an important role in offering specialized content to viewers and contributing to the diversity of programming available on television. Conditions of Licence may cover various aspects of broadcasting operations, including: Content Standards: Requirements related to the type of content that can be broadcast, such as restrictions on violence, explicit language, and discriminatory material. Canadian Content Quotas: Obligations to air a certain percentage of Canadian-produced content, including music, television programs, and films. Accessibility: Mandates to provide closed captioning, described video, and other accessibility features for viewers with disabilities. Local Programming: Requirements to produce and broadcast a minimum amount of local news, information, and community-focused programming. Financial Contributions: Obligations to invest in Canadian programming, such as Canadian Programming Expenditure (CPE) requirements. Reporting and Compliance: Responsibilities to submit reports, audits, and other documentation to demonstrate compliance with regulatory requirements. Failure to comply with the Conditions of Licence can result in penalties, fines, or the suspension or revocation of broadcasting licences. These conditions are put in place to uphold broadcasting standards, promote cultural diversity, support Canadian content, and serve the public interest in the media and entertainment industry. Each Canadian broadcaster has specific conditions of licence regarding the types of programs that they can broadcast, Canadian content requirements, either a general or detailed narrative description of the service and many other conditions related to the specific service. It utilizes a cyclic prefix, which is a copy of the end of each symbol, to guard against the effects of interference and multipath fading. GDPR imposes various obligations on organizations that process personal data, including the requirement to obtain consent, provide transparent information about data processing practices, implement appropriate security measures, and promptly notify individuals in the event of a data breach.

Name: GLP
Definition: The Group Licence Policy in the context of media and entertainment refers to a regulatory framework that governs the ownership and operation of multiple broadcasting services under a single corporate entity or group. This policy is often implemented by broadcasting regulators to oversee and regulate the activities of media companies that own and operate multiple television channels, radio stations, or other broadcasting platforms. Under the Group Licence Policy, broadcasting companies are granted a single licence that covers all of their broadcasting services within the group. This approach allows regulators to assess the overall performance, compliance, and impact of the group as a whole, rather than evaluating each individual service separately. It also provides a mechanism for regulators to monitor and enforce specific requirements related to content standards, diversity, Canadian content quotas, and other regulatory obligations across all services within the group. The Group Licence Policy aims to promote transparency, accountability, and diversity in the broadcasting industry by ensuring that media companies with multiple broadcasting services adhere to regulatory standards and contribute to the public interest. It helps regulators to oversee the operations of large media conglomerates and to maintain a balance between commercial interests and the broader societal goals of promoting cultural expression, diversity, and access to a variety of programming options for viewers. This is part of the CRTC 2010 policy that allowed broadcast corporate groups to be licensed as a group (ie Bell Media rather than CTV separate from CTV2, Space, Comedy etc.) and pool their CPE and PNI across the services in their group (on top of per service COLs).

Name: HARQ
Definition: Hybrid Automatic Repeat Request (HARQ) is a protocol used in telecommunications to improve the reliability of data transmission. It combines both error detection and error correction techniques to ensure that data is transmitted accurately and without loss. HARQ operates by dividing data into smaller packets and transmitting them individually. Upon receipt, the receiver acknowledges the correct packets and identifies any that have errors. The sender then retransmits only the erroneous packets, reducing network congestion and optimizing bandwidth utilization. This process continues until all packets are received correctly or the maximum number of retransmissions is reached. HARQ is an essential component in modern telecommunications systems to enhance data integrity and improve overall network performance.

Name: ID
Definition: Identity, in the context of General, refers to the characteristics, traits, or qualities that distinguish an individual or entity from others. It is the distinct set of personal or organizational attributes that define and represent who or what someone or something is.

Name: IDC

Name: iDEN

Name: IDM
Definition: Interactive Digital Media refers to digital content and experiences that allow users to actively engage with and participate in the content. This type of media goes beyond traditional forms of passive consumption, such as watching a movie or reading a book, and involves interactive elements that enable users to interact with the content in various ways. Interactive digital media can take many forms, including video games, virtual reality experiences, mobile apps, interactive websites, and multimedia presentations. These platforms often incorporate features like user input, decision-making, exploration, customization, and feedback mechanisms that make the content dynamic and engaging for the audience. The interactive nature of digital media allows users to have a more personalized and immersive experience, where their actions and choices can influence the outcome or direction of the content. This form of media blurs the line between creators and consumers, empowering users to actively participate in shaping their entertainment and learning experiences. Interactive digital media plays a significant role in the modern media landscape, offering new opportunities for storytelling, education, communication, and entertainment. It continues to evolve with advancements in technology, enabling innovative and interactive experiences that captivate and engage audiences in unique ways.

Name: IETF

Name: IHP

Name: IK
Definition: Integrity Key refers to a crucial element or code that ensures the preservation and accuracy of data or information, particularly in a general context. It acts as a safeguard to maintain the integrity and reliability of the data, ensuring that it remains intact and unaltered throughout its lifecycle. By employing an integrity key, organizations can validate the authenticity and trustworthiness of their data, thereby minimizing the risk of unauthorized modifications or tampering.

Name: IKEv2
Definition: Internet Key Exchange Version 2 (IKEv2) is a protocol used in the field of telecommunications. It allows for the secure exchange of cryptographic keys over an IP network, enabling the establishment of secure communication channels between devices. IKEv2 is designed to provide a reliable and efficient method for negotiating and managing security associations, which are essential for encrypting and authenticating data transmissions. It offers several security features and algorithms to ensure confidentiality, integrity, and authentication of the exchanged keys.

Name: ILEC
Definition: Incumbent Local Exchange Carrier refers to a telecommunications company that holds the dominant position in a specific local market. It typically has been established before competition is introduced and is regulated by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) in the United States. These carriers are responsible for providing basic telephone services to customers within their designated service areas.

Name: IMEI
Definition: This is a unique identifier for the mobile device itself and is typically 15 digits in length.

Name: IMS

It provides a framework for offering various communication services, such as voice, video, and data, through the integration of different networks and technologies. IMS allows for the seamless integration of both fixed and mobile networks, facilitating the convergence of various communication services into a single platform.

Name: IMSI
Definition: International Mobile Subscriber Identity (IMSI) is a unique numerical identifier used in telecommunications. It is assigned to each individual mobile subscriber globally and is stored on a SIM card. IMSI helps identify and authenticate mobile users on a network, allowing for seamless connectivity and secure communication.

Name: IMT

It encompasses the various systems and protocols that enable seamless communication between mobile devices across different countries and regions.

Name: IMT-2020

It represents the latest advancements and advancements in the field of mobile telecommunications, aiming to improve various aspects of mobile networks such as speed, capacity, connectivity, and efficiency. Name: IoT

Name: IP
Definition: The Internet Protocol (IP) is a protocol, or set of rules, for routing and addressing packets of data so that they can travel across networks and arrive at the correct destination. Data traversing the Internet is divided into smaller pieces, called packets. IP information is attached to each packet, and this information helps routers to send packets to the right place. Every device or domain that connects to the Internet is assigned an IP address , and as packets are directed to the IP address attached to them, data arrives where it is needed.

Name: IPP
Definition: Intrusion Protection System is a security mechanism designed to detect and prevent unauthorized access or malicious activities within a network or system. It actively monitors network traffic and identifies potential intrusion attempts, providing real-time alerts or implementing preventive measures to mitigate the risk.

Name: IPR

These rights enable the creators or owners to have exclusive control over the use, distribution, reproduction, or commercial exploitation of their intellectual property. Intellectual Property Rights aim to encourage innovation and creativity by providing a framework for creators to protect and profit from their creations.

Name: IPsec

IPsec provides authentication and encryption for data transmitted over network connections, protecting the confidentiality and integrity of the information being transmitted.

Name: IPTV

Name: IR

Name: IRAP
Definition: An Indigenous Reconciliation Action Plan is a strategic document that outlines an organization's commitment to advancing reconciliation with Indigenous peoples. These plans are typically developed by businesses, government agencies, educational institutions, and other organizations to promote understanding, respect, and positive relationships between Indigenous and non-Indigenous communities. Key components of a IRAP often include: Relationships : Building and maintaining respectful relationships with Indigenous communities and stakeholders. Respect : Promoting understanding and respect for Indigenous cultures, histories, and rights. Opportunities : Creating opportunities for Indigenous peoples in areas such as employment, education, and business. Governance and Reporting : Establishing governance structures to oversee the implementation of the RAP and reporting on progress. The IRAP framework is often guided by principles such as: Acknowledgment of Traditional Owners : Recognizing and respecting the Traditional Owners of the land. Cultural Competency : Providing training and education to increase cultural awareness and competency within the organization. Partnerships : Collaborating with Indigenous organizations and communities to support their goals and initiatives. Sustainability : Ensuring that reconciliation efforts are sustainable and have long-term impacts. Overall, an Indigenous Reconciliation Action Plan is a proactive approach to fostering reconciliation, addressing past injustices, and building a more inclusive and equitable future for Indigenous peoples.

Name: IRR
Definition: Internal Rate of Return (IRR) is a financial metric used in accounting and finance to evaluate the profitability and potential efficiency of an investment. It represents the discount rate at which the present value of future cash flows from the investment equals the initial cost of the investment. In other words, IRR is the rate of return that makes the net present value (NPV) of an investment equal to zero. A higher IRR indicates a more favorable investment opportunity, as it signifies a higher return on investment. IRR is commonly used by businesses and investors to compare various investment alternatives and make informed decisions about capital allocation. However, it is important to note that IRR does not consider the size or timing of cash flows and may not always provide a complete picture of an investment's potential risks and rewards.

Name: ISDN
Definition: Integrated Services Digital Network (ISDN) is a telecommunications technology that enables the transmission of digital data, voice, and video over traditional copper telephone lines. ISDN allows multiple services to be integrated and transmitted simultaneously, offering increased efficiency and flexibility in communication.

Name: ISG

Name: ISI

Name: ISM

It is used for applications in industrial, scientific, and medical fields, where wireless devices operate without interfering with licensed communication systems.

Name: ISP

ISPs enable users to connect to the internet by providing the necessary hardware and infrastructure. Major incident records are used to document and manage incidents that have a significant impact on operations, services, or stakeholders. Here are some key points about major incident records: Severity : Major incident records are reserved for incidents that have a high level of severity or impact on the organization. These incidents often disrupt normal operations, cause significant downtime, or have a widespread effect on services or customers. Response : Organizations use major incident records to track the response and resolution efforts for critical incidents. This includes documenting the actions taken, resources involved, communication strategies, and timelines for resolving the incident. Analysis : Major incident records are valuable for post-incident analysis and learning. They provide a detailed account of what happened, why it happened, and what steps were taken to mitigate the impact. This information can be used to improve incident response processes and prevent similar incidents in the future. Communication : Major incident records serve as a reference point for communication with stakeholders, management, and regulatory bodies. They provide a comprehensive overview of the incident and the organization's response to it. Overall, major incident records play a crucial role in incident management, ensuring that organizations can effectively respond to and recover from significant incidents while also learning from them to enhance future incident response capabilities.

It involves moving away from dedicated and specialized hardware devices and transitioning towards software-based solutions that can run on standard hardware. NFV allows network operators to deploy various network functions, such as firewalls, load balancers, and routers, as virtualized instances on generic servers. This enables greater flexibility, scalability, and cost-efficiency in the management and provisioning of network services. By decoupling network functions from proprietary hardware, NFV helps streamline network operations and facilitate the adoption of cloud-based services.

Name: NMBU
Definition: New Media Broadcasting Undertaking refers to an online platform or service that delivers audio or video content over the internet. These undertakings provide broadcasting services through digital platforms such as websites, streaming services, apps, and other online channels. The term "new media" distinguishes these platforms from traditional broadcasting methods like television and radio. In the context of media and entertainment regulation, a New Media Broadcasting Undertaking is subject to specific rules and requirements set by broadcasting authorities. These regulations may cover aspects such as content standards, licensing, Canadian content quotas, accessibility, and other obligations to ensure that online broadcasting services meet certain criteria for quality, diversity, and cultural representation. The emergence of New Media Broadcasting Undertakings has transformed the media landscape, offering viewers a wider range of content choices and on-demand access to programming. Regulators aim to adapt to these changes by extending their oversight to include online platforms to uphold broadcasting standards and promote the public interest in the digital age. These are broadcasting services that are offered over the Internet and through mobile services. they can be affiliated with a regulated broadcasting undertaking (e.g. cbc.ca) or unaffiliated (e.g. Netflix). They were originally defined under the 1999 New Media Exemption Order as amended in 2009 and renamed Digital Media Broadcasting Undertaking in 2012

Name: NoS
Definition: In the context of media and entertainment, "nature of service" refers to the type of content and programming that a broadcasting service offers to its audience. It encompasses the overall theme, format, genre, and target audience of the service. The nature of service is a key aspect of broadcasting regulations and licensing requirements, as it defines the scope and focus of the content that a broadcaster is permitted to air. Broadcasting regulators use the concept of "nature of service" to ensure that broadcasters adhere to specific guidelines and standards related to the type of content they provide. This includes considerations such as the diversity of programming, the representation of different perspectives, the protection of minors, and the promotion of Canadian content. By defining the nature of service, regulators can monitor and enforce compliance with broadcasting policies and regulations to uphold the public interest, diversity, and cultural objectives in the media and entertainment industry. It helps to maintain a balance between commercial interests and the broader societal goals of promoting cultural expression, diversity, and access to a variety of programming options for viewers. Nature of Service are part of the conditions of licence (COL) for specialty services which define the kind of programming that they can broadcast. Sometimes they are very specific (i.e. science fiction and fantasy) and other times very vague (the best of drama).

Name: NPBCH

Name: NPSS

It helps the receiving device or system to synchronize with the transmitting device or system, ensuring that data is transmitted and received accurately. The signal contains important timing and frequency information that allows the receiving device to adjust its own internal clock and frequency to match that of the transmitting device. This synchronization is crucial for successful communication and data transmission between devices in a telecommunications network.

Definition: Net Present Value is a financial metric used in the context of General. It is a measure used to assess the profitability or value of an investment by comparing the present value of cash inflows with the present value of cash outflows. It takes into account the time value of money, considering that a dollar received in the future is worth less than a dollar received today. By discounting future cash flows to their present value, Net Present Value helps determine the net value or profitability of an investment after accounting for the cost of capital.

Definition: Non-Simultaneous Substitution refers to a practice in the broadcasting industry where a broadcaster replaces a program or advertisement in a broadcast with a different program or advertisement at a later time. This practice is often used to provide viewers with content that is more relevant or appealing to the local audience or to maximize advertising revenue. In the context of media and entertainment, non-simultaneous substitution can occur when a broadcaster decides to air a different program in place of the original one during a repeat broadcast or in a time-shifted viewing scenario. This practice allows broadcasters to tailor content to specific audiences or to optimize their advertising strategies based on viewer demographics or preferences. Non-simultaneous substitution can also be used to address scheduling conflicts, regional preferences, or other factors that may impact the viewership experience. It is a common strategy employed by broadcasters to enhance viewer engagement and to better meet the needs of their audience. Non-Simultaneous Substitution is also known as Simulcast or Simsub or Simultaneous Substitution is a CRTC policy that allows Canadian broadcasters to broadcast US feeds – at the same time as the US feed – while stripping out the US ads so that they can sell the ad time to Canadian advertisers. It allows Canadian broadcasters to tape the feed, strip out the US ads, sell the ad time to Canadian advertisers and broadcast the US feed at the time of their choosing.

Definition: The Open Radio Access Network (Open RAN) is a concept in the telecommunications industry that aims to disaggregate the traditional RAN (Radio Access Network) components by using open and interoperable interfaces and standards. This approach allows operators to mix and match hardware and software components from different vendors, promoting vendor diversity and innovation. Open RAN architecture typically includes the following key components: Radio Unit (RU) : The hardware that connects to the antennas and converts digital signals to radio waves. Distributed Unit (DU) : Responsible for baseband processing and control functions. Centralized Unit (CU) : Handles higher-layer processing and network management functions. Open Interfaces : Standardized interfaces that allow interoperability between different vendors' components. By adopting Open RAN, operators can potentially reduce costs, increase flexibility, and accelerate innovation in the deployment of mobile networks. It also promotes competition and avoids vendor lock-in, leading to a more dynamic and diverse ecosystem in the telecommunications industry.
